items.stem: You take a slice of a NumPy array and modify it; the original array also changes. Why?

options.text: Basic slicing returns a view that shares memory with the original
options.rationale: Correct: basic slicing yields a view onto the same underlying data, so edits propagate.

options.text: NumPy copies arrays on every slice
options.rationale: Basic slicing returns a view, not a copy.
This is expected view behavior, not corruption.

options.text: Slicing is not allowed on arrays
options.rationale: Slicing is fully supported on arrays.

items.explanation: Correct: basic slicing yields a view onto the same underlying data, so edits propagate.

items.stem: Adding a shape (3,) vector to a shape (4,3) matrix works because of which NumPy feature?

options.rationale: Correct: broadcasting stretches the vector across the matrix's rows.
Transposition changes axes order; it is not why the add works.
Sorting is unrelated to element-wise addition.
Concatenation joins arrays; it does not add them.

items.explanation: Correct: broadcasting stretches the vector across the matrix's rows.

items.stem: Which TWO statements about NumPy aggregation are correct? (Select TWO)

options.text: axis=0 reduces along rows, collapsing each column
options.rationale: Correct: axis=0 collapses the row dimension, giving a per-column result.

options.text: Omitting axis aggregates over the entire array
options.rationale: Correct: with no axis, the reduction spans all elements to one value.
axis=0 returns an array per column, not a single scalar in general.

options.text: Reductions cannot be applied to 2D arrays
options.rationale: Reductions apply to arrays of any dimensionality.
